source.snippet: LLM output, according to court rulings IIUC, cannot be copyrighted. This should worry both proprietary software companies and open source projects alike (because you can't put a license on something you don't hold the rights for). Yet, even Linux is accepting LLM-generated code. Do they (not just Linux) have a plan? [4 points, 2 comments]

problem_statement: Software teams and open-source projects shipping LLM-generated code lack tooling to track, flag, or document which code segments are AI-generated, creating legal exposure around copyright ownership and license compliance that auditors and enterprise buyers increasingly demand proof of.
target_segment: Engineering leads and legal/compliance teams at software companies (10–5000 employees) and open-source foundations shipping products with LLM-assisted code
notes: Early signal — only 4 points but the question surfaces a real and growing legal gap as AI coding tools mainstream. Enterprise buyers (CTOs, GCs) already asking vendors for SBOM-equivalent AI provenance docs. No clear paid tool exists yet for 'AI content fraction' auditing in repos. Willingness-to-pay likely tied to enterprise legal review cycles.
